result.explanation: Two identical $8,157.60 Fastenal payments posted the same day, but the descriptions cite different invoice numbers (OKMCA199194 and OKMCA199188). That points to two separate invoices rather than a duplicate. Identical amounts on consecutive invoices is unusual, though, and the amount is far above the $356 merchant median. Fastenal is a routine supplier for this card (53 purchases). Someone should check both invoices against Fastenal's statement.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: Two distinct invoices (OKMCA199194 and OKMCA199188) of coincidentally equal amount, e.g. recurring identical orders, paid the same day.

result.explanation: A $5,000 Lowe's purchase of three "GIFT CARD EA" lines is the largest transaction on a card whose median is $155 and which is mostly ads, Amazon and software. The data has no sign of an employee-recognition program. The Lottery Commission has 9 Lowe's purchases (median $2,000) across 2 cards, so gift-card buying may be recurring. Recognition is an allowed exception, so someone should ask for documentation.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.d — Gift Certificates (except purchases for employee recognition)
result.innocent_explanation: The gift cards may have been bought for an approved employee recognition or incentive program, which the policy allows.

result.explanation: The card looks like an athletics travel card. It has team meals, catering, athletic purchases and event tickets. A large hotel group-room charge fits that use. The merchant has only one earlier purchase ($18,070.42), on this same card and agency, so lodging here is not new. The size is unusual, but "ROOM CHARGES" is a lodging description and I saw nothing personal. I did not see an itinerary or a duplicate charge.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use: goods or services for personal use and not for official State use
result.innocent_explanation: A team or group lodging block for athletics travel, billed as one folio. Hotel room charges for many people can reach this size.

result.explanation: MMS GOV SOLUTION is this card's top merchant (883 of 2,232 transactions). The Veterans Affairs agency spends $1.5M there across 6 cards. The 25 purchases are varied medical supplies, mostly small, with a median near $400, and the card shows the same daily pattern in August. That looks like routine replenishment from a regular supplier. I saw no sign of intent to divide a known quantity. Several lines look like different orders, not one split item.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing (requires known quantity and intent to evade $5,000 limit)
result.innocent_explanation: Routine daily medical supply restocking for a veterans facility from its regular supplier. Each order was a different product and was placed separately as needs arose.

result.explanation: Card's median purchase is $260, yet 22+ Amazon orders for the same baby items (car seats, Pack n Plays, cabinet locks, teethers) hit within 3 days, several just under $5,000 (T202510031897 $4,939.86). The burst continues past 10/24. It looks like one known quantity split across orders, but a bulk program purchase can't be ruled out. Needs a check of the business purpose and any exemption.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing
result.innocent_explanation: A planned bulk purchase of infant-safety supplies for a clinic, child-care or community program (the card also shows a children's charity payment), placed as many separate Amazon orders for different sellers or delivery addresses. Amazon is the card's normal merchant.

result.explanation: The 16 charges are different electrical parts (clamps, cutouts, terminations, wire) bought from a regular supplier. Border States is used only by this agency (182 purchases, median $1,447.68), so high volume is normal. The data doesn't show one known quantity of a single item being divided. The two $1,418.33 charges have different descriptions (500R vs 2500 FT wire), so they are not a clear double charge. The charges look like invoice lines.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing (requires intent to divide a known quantity)
result.innocent_explanation: A utility restocked line-construction materials in one order, and the vendor billed each line item as its own charge. The items are different parts, and some of the individual charges are large.

result.explanation: Fentanyl test strips are a plausible Health Department public-health purchase, from a vendor this card uses often (TFS Fisher Sci RAR, 28 purchases). That makes the personal-use flag unlikely. But $69,770 is a single charge, about 6x the card's next largest ($10,981.62) and far over the $5,000 limit. No listed exemption clearly applies. Someone should confirm the contract, approval, or exemption.
result.policy_clause: OMES P-Card Procedures §IV.D — $5,000 single item purchase limit (74 O.S. § 85.5a)
result.innocent_explanation: A bulk public-health order of fentanyl test strips for harm-reduction programs, bought under a statewide contract or exemption, or as many low-cost units that each fall under the limit.

result.explanation: A $5,000 Amazon physical gift card is the card's largest purchase (median $250). It came one day after a $1,250 physical gift card. Earlier eGift cards were $150–$350. Gift cards are allowed only for employee recognition, and nothing in the data shows a recognition program. Recognition is plausible in December, but the size and the physical format need documentation of recipients and purpose.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.d — Gift Certificates (except purchases for employee recognition)
result.innocent_explanation: Year-end employee recognition or award program purchased through Amazon gift cards, which the policy permits.

result.explanation: A single $8,304.75 charge at a service station (HARRIS 33) is far above the card's $573 median. It is the only purchase at this merchant by any card or agency, and it has no fuel detail. The card is otherwise used for truck and equipment parts and service, so bulk fuel for a fleet is possible. But the amount is unusually large for fuel and the policy allows fuel only for state-owned vehicles. A person should check the receipt.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.e — Motor Fuel or Fluids; the ComData card must be used for fuel for state-owned vehicles
result.innocent_explanation: Bulk fuel or fluids for the agency's state-owned trucks and equipment fleet, which this card often services. It may also be a fuel-related service or equipment charge coded as a service station.

result.explanation: A $4,500 Amazon gift card is far above this card's median purchase ($50) and its usual Amazon gift cards ($5–$100). It came two days after a $1,500 Target gift card ("YOU ARE THE BEST"). That pattern fits an employee recognition program, which the policy allows, but nothing in the data shows one. Someone should ask for the recognition program documentation and the recipient list.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.d — Gift Certificates (except purchases for employee recognition)
result.innocent_explanation: A bulk employee or student recognition award, which is exempt, bought as one large gift card order near the holidays. The card's earlier small gift cards and the Target "YOU ARE THE BEST" gift card point the same way.

result.explanation: The card has 868 Amazon purchases across 1,144 transactions, and the January 2025 history shows the same heavy buying pattern. The 34 charges are mostly unrelated items from different marketplace sellers: cameras, audio gear, books, furniture, office supplies. They aren't one divided known quantity. Individual amounts stay under $5,000, and no single order was visibly split. This looks like a media-production or departmental purchasing card buying routinely, so I found no sign of intent to evade the limit.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing (requires a known quantity and intent to evade the $5,000 limit)
result.innocent_explanation: A university department made routine, varied Amazon purchases for a studio, classroom or office setup. The orders were separate, from different sellers, for different items. The $34.6K total over six days is a bulk equipment and supplies buy, not a divided single purchase.

result.explanation: Two identical $21,700.00 Fastenal charges posted 2025-05-14 with different invoice numbers (OKADA123890 and OKADA123899), which suggests two real invoices rather than a duplicate posting. However, the identical round amount is odd. A $21,700.00 charge also appeared 2025-04-15 (invoice OKADA123404). DOT is a heavy Fastenal buyer. Confirm both invoices with Fastenal and recover the money if one is a duplicate.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: Two separate invoices with distinct numbers, each paid at a recurring fixed amount (a $21,700.00 payment also appeared in April), for a regular DOT supplier.

result.explanation: A $271.56 work boot purchase at WORKBOOTS.COM is out of pattern for this card, which mostly pays utilities, telecom, cable and software. It is the card's only shoe purchase. The data doesn't show whether it was for official use. Another agency made an identical-amount purchase there. Safety footwear can be a legitimate work expense, so a reviewer should check for a business purpose and who the boots were for.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use: goods or services for personal use and not for official State use
result.innocent_explanation: Required safety or work boots for facilities, grounds or maintenance staff, bought online for official use. A matching $271.56 purchase at another agency suggests a standard price for one item.

result.explanation: A $6,416.23 fuel purchase on a purchase card. Policy §V.B.1.e prohibits motor fuel or fluids, and state vehicles must use the ComData fuel card. Nothing else on this card is fuel; it mostly buys industrial supplies. The amount is the largest at this merchant. The agency has used this merchant twice before ($8,868.68 across 3 purchases on 2 cards). The fuel may be bulk fuel for equipment or non-state vehicles, which a reviewer should confirm.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.e — Motor Fuel or Fluids; FAQ: the ComData card must be used for fuel for state-owned vehicles
